transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for calling S-Net customer technical support, my name is Martin. How can I help you today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hello Martin. Our landline telephone has developed an unbearable crackling and hissing noise on the line. When anyone calls, there is so much static that you can barely hear a word, and our broadband speed has dropped by half as well!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I can help you diagnose that line noise, Joanne. First let's complete security verification. What is your full name and the installation address?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Joanne Briggs, 22 Willow Brook, Preston, PR2 1TY.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And what is the security PIN on the account, Joanne?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: What type of telephone handset is currently plugged into the phone socket?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: We have a Panasonic cordless base station with two handsets.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Does the loud crackling sound persist when you unplug the cordless base station and try a standard corded phone?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I tried an old corded telephone from the attic, and the crackling was just as loud.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I will run an automated line test across the copper pair from our Preston exchange. Bear with me for forty seconds.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for your patience, Joanne. The line test has completed. It shows a severe resistive loop fault of eighty thousand ohms, indicating either dampness or a faulty extension socket.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: We haven't had any building work or leaks inside the house. Could it be the street wiring?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: To isolate internal house wiring from the external Openreach street cable, we need to test from your master socket test socket.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Where is the master socket located?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It's usually in the main hallway where the telephone line enters the property.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, I am looking at the white box in the hall with the S-Net logo on it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Does the faceplate have a horizontal line split across the middle with two small screws?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, two little screws on the bottom half.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Use a small coin or flat screwdriver to unscrew those two screws and pull the bottom faceplate gently forward.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: We have had this terrible line noise for three days and it was driving my husband crazy! We couldn't hear our doctor on the phone!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Internal copper wiring issues can indeed create substantial audio interference.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'm just glad we didn't have to wait a week for an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Testing at the master socket resolves roughly seventy percent of residential noise reports immediately.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's such a clever design having a test socket behind the faceplate.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And modern routers have built-in microfilters that reject residual radio frequency interference.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Good to know the hardware is protected.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And you can always check your line performance using our automated line checker tool on the My S-Net portal.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'll bookmark that tool on my iPad.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Unscrewing them now... Pulling the faceplate off. Behind it, there is another hidden telephone socket inside!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That hidden socket is the master test socket. It connects directly to the incoming street wire, completely disconnecting all internal extension cables.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What should I plug into it?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let me check the equipment setup again. What type of telephone handset do you have there to plug in?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: As I told you at the start, I have the Panasonic cordless telephone.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Plug the Panasonic cordless phone directly into that internal test socket.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Plugging the phone cable into the test socket... Putting handset to my ear.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Do you hear a dial tone, and is there any static or crackling?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The dial tone is completely silent and crystal clear! Absolutely zero crackling or hissing!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That is fantastic news. That proves the external Openreach street cable is one hundred percent healthy, and the fault was caused by internal extension wiring.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Looking at the back of the faceplate I removed, there is an old rusty bell-wire terminal that looks corroded!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Old bell-wire ring capacitors in extension faceplates often corrode with age, injecting high resistance onto the VDSL circuit.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Can I just leave the extension bell-wire disconnected?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, modern cordless phones do not use old bell-wires. Gently unclip the orange and white extension wires from terminals 2 and 5.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Unclipped both wires and wrapped them with insulating tape.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Now screw the master faceplate back on, and plug your broadband microfilter and phone back into the front.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Screwed faceplate back on... Plugged filter, phone, and router back in.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Pick up the phone and check the dial tone now.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Holding phone to ear... Perfect, clean, silent dial tone! And my router broadband light just turned solid green!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let me re-run the exchange copper line test from my screen. Bear with me for thirty seconds.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thanks for holding, Joanne. The resistive fault has cleared completely to infinite resistance, and your VDSL sync speed has jumped back up to sixty-eight megabits.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That is an astonishing fix Martin. You saved us an eighty-pound Openreach callout fee!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I will take direct ownership of this ticket and note that the internal bell-wire was safely isolated.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you Martin, I really appreciate your patience in guiding me through that.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Just to confirm your billing contact email on file, it's joanne dot briggs at preston dot co dot uk, correct?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, that's my email.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Just to confirm for the ticket record, the installation address is 22 Willow Brook, correct?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, 22 Willow Brook.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Is there anything else with your telephone or broadband that I can assist you with today, Joanne?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No Martin, the crackle is completely gone and internet speed is doubled. Thank you so much.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for choosing S-Net, Joanne, and have a lovely afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you Martin, goodbye.
